samples.summary: Parquet import decodes an attacker-supplied file with no row/cell budget — a compression bomb turns a ≤50 MB upload into unbounded memory allocation (client-side DoS)
samples.evidence: Vector: an attacker sends a victim a `.parquet` file (mail/Slack/shared drive); the victim drops it into the documents list. `enqueue()` only checks byte size (`uploadSizeError`, packages/frontend/src/app/documents/file-meta.ts:34, cap 50 MB for kind "sheet"), then `importParquet` reads the whole file and calls `parquetReadObjects({ file, compressors })` (parquet-importer.ts:23) with no `rowStart`/`rowEnd` bound. Parquet is columnar + dictionary/RLE encoded and, with the newly wired GZIP/ZSTD/Snappy codecs (hyparquet-compressors), a 50 MB file can legitimately expand to hundreds of GB of decoded JS objects — hyparquet materializes ALL rows as objects before this code sees them. `importRecordsAsSheet` (packages/sheets/src/import/record-importer.ts:35-74) then writes every cell with no cap either. Contrast the CSV path, which enforces `MAX_IMPORT_CELLS` (40,000) AND a byte budget precisely because an unbounded import is unrecoverable (packages/sheets/src/import/csv-importer.ts:155, 288); the design doc for this feature also lists "Huge files bloating the Yorkie document → Materialize cap" as a required mitigation (docs/design/sheets/file-import.md:173). Impact: browser tab OOM/hang during import, and — if it survives — an oversized document pushed at `applyContent`/Yorkie (packages/frontend/src/app/documents/upload-queue.ts:359). XLSX/JSON share the missing budget (csv-importer.ts:163 acknowledges it), but Parquet is the first format whose compression ratio makes it cheap to weaponize.

samples.summary: Untrusted Parquet/JSON string values beginning with `=` are committed as live formula cells; the CSV importer deliberately neutralizes exactly this and the shared record importer does not
samples.evidence: Vector: an attacker puts the string `=HYPERLINK("https://evil.example","Payroll Q3")` (or any formula) in a Parquet string column and sends the file to a victim. `importRecordsAsSheet` passes every value straight to `cellFromInput(toCell(value))` (record-importer.ts:63); `inferInput` classifies a leading `=` as a formula (packages/sheets/src/model/worksheet/input.ts:235) and `cellFromInput` stores `{ f: normalizeFormulaOnCommit(...) }` (input.ts:354-359), so the untrusted text becomes an executable formula in a shared, collaboratively-edited document rather than inert text. The CSV importer explicitly refuses to do this — `toImportCell` returns `{ v: trimmed }` for a leading `=` (packages/sheets/src/import/csv-importer.ts:71-73) — so the two import paths now disagree on whether file content may author formulas. Exfiltration reach looks limited (no IMPORTDATA/WEBSERVICE in the catalog; HYPERLINK only returns its label, packages/sheets/src/formula/functions-lookup.ts:918), which is why this is minor rather than higher, but the formula-injection surface (spoofed labels, recalculation cost, future network-capable functions) is real and the code moved by this diff extends it to a new attacker-supplied binary format.

samples.summary: Hardening: three new transitive binary-parsing dependencies (hyparquet, hyparquet-compressors → fzstd, hysnappy/WASM) parse fully untrusted attacker-supplied bytes on the app's main thread in the document origin
samples.evidence: The change adds `hyparquet` and `hyparquet-compressors` (pulling `fzstd` and the WASM-based `hysnappy`, pnpm-lock.yaml:7112-7120) and feeds them raw user file bytes with no format/soundness pre-check of our own (parquet-importer.ts:23). The parse runs synchronously on the main thread in the same origin as the editor (no Web Worker isolation, unlike nothing else here), so any parser bug is at minimum a full-tab hang and the codecs are the least-audited part of the new surface. `pnpm audit` only fails this repo on CRITICAL advisories, so a high/moderate advisory in any of these four packages would land silently. Suggest running the decode in a worker and pinning/monitoring these deps.

verdict.reason: The absence claim is factually accurate — I confirmed there is no row/cell budget anywhere on the Parquet path: parquet-importer.ts:21 calls parquetReadObjects with no rowStart/rowEnd, record-importer.ts:46-74 uses cellCount purely as a report and never as a bound, sheet-import-actions.ts:118-127 returns no truncated/rowCount (and its own comment at lines 17-25 says only CSV has a budget), and the only pre-import gate is the 50 MB byte cap at file-meta.ts:34-48. No counterexample exists. However it is not blocking under the Security lens: the vector crosses no trust or privilege boundary — a user voluntarily imports a local file and the worst outcome is memory exhaustion in their own browser tab, recoverable by closing it. There is no authorization, secret, injection, crypto/signature, SSRF or path-traversal element, and "unsafe deserialization" in the security sense means gadget/code execution, not allocation volume; resource-exhaustion DoS is not in this lens's enumerated lane. The one place it could become shared-resource impact is already guarded server-side: Yorkie enforces MaxSizePerDocument = 10485760 and doc.update() throws "document size exceeds the limit" (documented/measured at csv-doc-size.test.ts:10-31), so an oversized document cannot be persisted via applyImportedContent (apply-imported-content.ts:207-218). Nor is this a security control that was added-but-bypassable or moved off the enforced path — there is no gate to bypass; it is a materialize-cap/robustness gap of the same shape the repo already documents as accepted for XLSX and JSON. Refuted on scope only: a correctness or resource-limits reviewer should keep this item.
